tasks.short: Count prisoners in cells and units, write the count on the count sheet, compare it with the expected roll and resolve differences, and report the count to the control room.

steps.what: Correctional officer conducts head counts to ensure that each prisoner is present
Correctional officer writes the count on the count sheet
Correctional officer compares the count with the expected roll and resolves differences
Correctional officer reports the count to the control room by radio

tasks.design: The officer enters the count per unit on a handheld linked to the prisoner administration ({OPS_SYSTEM}), which computes the expected roll from that day's transfers, court visits and hospital stays and shows any difference at once. Once the officer has cleared the count, it goes to the control room screen instead of by radio. Counting each prisoner in person stays with the officer.
tasks.previous_blocker: Counts were written on sheets and expected numbers worked out by hand from movement lists.
tasks.enabler_now: Prisoner administration systems track movements and can compute the expected roll.
tasks.still_hard: Late movements not yet entered cause false differences.
tasks.human_edge: Checking that a figure under a blanket is breathing.

evidence.claim: Handheld count entry can be compared with an expected roll computed from recorded movements.
Systems that can monitor staff need works council consent.

assumptions: Boundary: from the count time to the count reported; searches after a wrong count are outside.
Input contract: movements entered in the prisoner administration; fallback is sheets and radio.
Counting in person does not change.

incremental.description: Correctional officer enters late movements before the count.

approvals.approved_version: The count as cleared by the officer in s3.

time_saved_range_pct.basis: Low: a small unit with few movements; high: a large unit with many daily movements.

tasks.savings_basis: 100 focal-role baseline hours; external labour excluded; incremental focal work deducted once; provisional

tasks.short: Watch prisoners in the housing unit and during work and recreation, watch camera screens, and write observation notes on behavior.

steps.what: Correctional officer monitors conduct of prisoners in the housing unit and during work or recreational activities
Correctional officer watches camera screens to prevent escape or violence
Correctional officer writes observation notes on behavior

tasks.design: Observation notes go into the prisoner file on a handheld ({OPS_SYSTEM}) with pick lists for common behavior, instead of a paper notebook copied later. Watching prisoners and screens stays with the officer; no software predicts or scores prisoners' behavior.
tasks.previous_blocker: Notes were written in notebooks and copied into the file later.
tasks.enabler_now: Handheld entry into prisoner files is common.
tasks.still_hard: Tension builds in ways no note captures.
tasks.human_edge: Sensing that a unit is about to turn.

reach.learn: Whether notes are in the file the same day.

evidence.claim: Offence prediction based solely on profiling is banned under AI Act article 5(1)(d); here no software scores prisoners.

assumptions: Boundary: from the unit routine to observation notes; disciplinary decisions are outside.
Input contract: prisoner files in the administration system; fallback is notebooks.
Watching prisoners and screens does not change.
research_questions: Are notes complete at shift handover more often?

incremental.description: Correctional officer learns the handheld note entry.

time_saved_range_pct.basis: Low: few notes per shift; high: a unit with many notes.

tasks.savings_basis: 100 focal-role baseline hours; external labour excluded; incremental focal work deducted once; provisional

tasks.short: Search prisoners, vehicles and cells for contraband, record found items and seizures, and hand seized items over with paperwork.

steps.what: Correctional officer searches prisoners and vehicles and conducts shakedowns of cells for contraband
Correctional officer records found items and seizures on a paper form
Correctional officer hands seized items over with paperwork

tasks.design: Seizures are recorded on a handheld form ({OPS_SYSTEM}) with a photo and a barcode label for each bag, so the chain of custody does not depend on handwritten forms. Searching stays with the officer.
tasks.previous_blocker: Seizures were written on paper forms that travelled with the bag.
tasks.enabler_now: Handheld forms with photos and barcode labels are common in evidence handling.
tasks.still_hard: Contraband is hidden in new ways all the time.
tasks.human_edge: Knowing where in a cell something does not belong.

evidence.claim: Handheld forms with photos and barcode labels can record seized items.

assumptions: Boundary: from the search order to items handed over; prosecution is outside.
Input contract: forms set by the security department; fallback is paper.
research_questions: Do seizure records reach security the same day?

incremental.description: Correctional officer prints and attaches barcode labels.

time_saved_range_pct.basis: Low: few seizures; high: many searches with finds.

tasks.savings_basis: 100 focal-role baseline hours; external labour excluded; incremental focal work deducted once; provisional

tasks.short: Record prisoner identification and charges at intake, keep daily logs of prisoner activities, write incident reports on disturbances, check and sign them, and send them to the unit manager.

steps.what: Correctional officer records prisoner identification and charges at intake
Correctional officer keeps daily logs of prisoner activities on paper
Correctional officer writes reports on incidents of inmate disturbance
Correctional officer checks and signs the incident report
Correctional officer e-mails the signed report to the unit manager

tasks.design: Identification and charges arrive with the transfer from police or court and prefill the intake record in the prisoner administration ({OPS_SYSTEM}); the officer checks them against the person. Daily activities are logged on a handheld with pick lists instead of paper. Incident reports use a structured form with the prisoners, place and time filled from the log. Once the officer has signed the report, it goes to the unit manager. Writing what happened stays with the officer.
tasks.previous_blocker: Transfer papers were retyped, logs kept on paper and reports written from scratch.
tasks.enabler_now: Transfer data can prefill intake records; handhelds take structured logs.
tasks.still_hard: Reports on violence must be precise and fair, so writing them takes care.
tasks.human_edge: Describing a fight so that it is clear who started it.
tasks.altitude: The officer checks prefilled records instead of retyping.

reach.learn: Whether reports arrive complete the same day.

evidence.claim: Axon's report tool drafts patrol reports from body camera audio; officers clear flagged passages and confirm.
Systems that can monitor staff, such as time-stamped logs, need works council consent.

assumptions: Boundary: from transfer papers to the report sent; disciplinary hearings are outside.
Input contract: transfer data from police and courts; fallback is paper and retyping.
Writing and signing reports stay with the officer; no model drafts incident reports here.
research_questions: Do intake errors fall when data are prefilled?

incremental.description: Correctional officer corrects prefilled data that do not match the person.

approvals.approved_version: The incident report as checked and signed by the officer in s4.

time_saved_range_pct.basis: Low: a small unit with few intakes; high: a remand centre with many intakes.

tasks.savings_basis: 100 focal-role baseline hours; external labour excluded; incremental focal work deducted once; provisional

role.altitude: The correctional officer keeps counting, watching, searching and writing what happened; count sheets, paper logs and retyped papers shrink.
role.ambitious_version: An officer with more time on the unit floor.
